title: Should I move from a snowflake environment to a fabric environment to get back to a DE role?
summary: I have been a DE for over 10 years working on SSIS and later building pipelines on databricks and dbt. Earlier this year I took up a new job as a manager of an analytics team. I hate my role and the lack of ownership and hands on work. I am primarily tasked with leading a team on reporting and data delivery and semantic layer while depending on the DE team for all data. I am also not enjoying middle management. Current job is a snowflake, dbt and AWS shop but I am my team primarily just write sql on snowflake. Recently I have been in conversations for a data architect role at another team in my organization and it’s a more engineering and architecture focused role which I want but they use Fabric. Wondering if that makes a difference. I am inclined to take the new role if it works out just so I can move out of analytics and go back to a more data engineering focused IC role. submitted by /u/Throwaway081920231 [link] [comments]

title: Inside the long, bitter fight over one man’s quest to build the biggest AI datacenter in California
summary: A modern-day prospector promised rural Imperial thousands of jobs and millions in tax revenue – but his plan has set off a firestorm of resistance Sebastian Rucci zoomed in on a map in late 2024, looking closely at a large block of brown earth. The barren plot sandwiched between sprawling alfalfa fields and sleepy desert suburbs was exactly what he’d been searching for – the perfect place to realize his dream of building the largest artificial intelligence datacenter in California. The dusty expanse wasn’t an obvious location. It was in the Sonoran desert, just north of the Mexican border, where temperatures regularly rose past 100F (37.8C). Water was scarce in the once-booming agricultural area, which gets its supply from the beleaguered Colorado River. And then, there was the city of Imperial – population 22,000 – to win over. As controversial datacenter projects have sprung up across the US, residents were naturally skeptical of a new, energy-guzzling neighbor. Continue reading...

title: Fake Linda and me: the Agatha Christie-worthy mystery of the fraudster who stole my byline
summary: How a string of bizarre events led writer Linda Geddes to don her sleuthing cap and dig into a world of shadowy impersonators It started with an entirely ordinary interaction on LinkedIn. Someone had tagged me in a post, saying how much they’d enjoyed contributing to a New York Post article I’d written about “chronoworking”. As the author of a book about circadian rhythms, it was exactly the sort of subject I might write about. Except I’d never heard of this person, let alone interviewed them. I clicked on the link and my stomach dropped. There, above an article about people who organise their working lives around their biological clocks, was my name: Linda Geddes. Continue reading...
